title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
This page holds §§X–XII of E297. Euler is laying the methodological groundwork for re-deriving, by Lagrange's δ-method, the rule (later called the Euler–Lagrange equation) for extremizing A = ∫_0^a Z dx. Z may depend on x, y, higher derivatives of y and embedded integrals.

§X: an extremum requires that every infinitesimal variation of the ordinates y produce zero change in A, whatever the variations are. It would therefore suffice to vary a single ordinate y at one point. That was the basis of Euler's earlier method (Methodus inveniendi, 1744). Yet even if many, or all, ordinates are varied arbitrarily, the change in A must still vanish.

§XI: varying only one ordinate while all the others stay fixed 'does violence to the principle of continuity'. That is why the earlier investigation could not be carried out purely analytically. It needed a geometric figure, with ordinates as lines of a curve, to work out how the differential ratios dy/dx, d²y/dx², … change. To avoid violating continuity, Euler now gives every ordinate an infinitesimal variation. These variations are left indefinite, so they can later be fixed at will; in particular all but one can be set to zero, which recovers the old solutions.

§XII: varying all ordinates arbitrarily makes the method broader than the old one. If the variations are restricted in some definite way, one can solve problems where the extremal is sought not among all curves but only among an infinite family of curves of a given 'species'. Euler says such problems are usually very hard, and further advances in analysis may be expected.

In modern terms, this is the passage from a pointwise, discretized variation (a bump at one node of a polygonal curve) to a smooth variation field δy(x). It amounts to the first variation, or Gâteaux derivative, in an arbitrary direction. The same paper's next page introduces δ as an operator distinct from d. Restricting the admissible variations corresponds to optimizing over a constrained submanifold of curves.
errors: No mathematical errors. The claim that a single-ordinate variation 'violates continuity' is heuristic. In the 1744 method it is legitimate once the variation is understood as a discrete node perturbation. Euler's point is about analytic convenience, not validity.
The claim in §X that varying one ordinate suffices is not by itself a rigorous derivation of the necessary condition for smooth functionals. It needs the later fundamental lemma (du Bois-Reymond).

ideas.what: Variation of all ordinates simultaneously by an arbitrary infinitesimal field δy, instead of one ordinate
ideas.modern_name: first variation / Gâteaux derivative in arbitrary direction
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1755 letter to Euler; 1760–61 Miscellanea Taurinensia), adopted and named by Euler
ideas.where_published: E296 Elementa calculi variationum (1766); E297; later Institutiones calculi integralis vol. 3 appendix (E385)

ideas.what: Critique of the 1744 single-ordinate method as conflicting with the 'principle of continuity' and needing geometric aids
ideas.modern_name: discretized (polygonal) direct method vs analytic variational calculus
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler's self-assessment; discussed by Goldstine and Fraser
ideas.where_published: E296/E297 introductions; Goldstine, History of the Calculus of Variations (1980); Fraser's papers on Euler and Lagrange

ideas.what: Restricting the variations to a specified mode yields extremal problems over a restricted 'species' of curves
ideas.modern_name: constrained variational problems / optimization over a submanifold or parametrized family of admissible curves
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Lagrange (isoperimetric and relative extrema); later the Ritz method for finite-parameter families
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi ch. 5–6 (relative maxima); E297 and related memoirs

deep.surprise_reason: This is a well-known programmatic passage in which Euler adopts Lagrange's δ-method and contrasts it with his 1744 method. Historians of the calculus of variations (Goldstine, Fraser, Opera omnia I.25 introduction) have thoroughly covered it. The remark in §XII on restricted families of curves is suggestive but generic.
